title: Lighthouse SDK kits: concise Next.js / FastAPI / Go HTTP / CLI examples with retry & streaming best-practices
creator: Aisha Malik
description: Deliver a small collection of opinionated starter kits (Next.js web app, FastAPI backend, Go HTTP microservice, and a cross-platform CLI) demonstrating recommended Redwood SDK patterns for: (1) ergonomic streaming, (2) robust retry/backoff and idempotency, (3) token-aware batching hints, and (4) clear examples for structured output and function/tool calling. Each kit will include a short README, a minimal runnable app, a CI-ready test that exercises streaming and retries, and a short cookbook snippet explaining trade-offs. The goal is to give users minimal friction examples that they can copy-paste into a new project and extend.
tasks: Design minimal API surface for streaming in each language (sync vs async variants in Python)
Implement Next.js example demonstrating streaming tokens to browser and fallback to polling for slow connections
Implement FastAPI example that showcases request proxying, retry + idempotency headers, and streaming SSE support
Implement Go HTTP server showing context cancellation, chunked streaming, and server-side batching advice
Build CLI wrapper (TS or Go) that exercises retries with exponential backoff and exposes a --stream flag
Write acceptance tests that validate retry behavior (idempotency key honored) and streaming resiliency (client reconnect)
Create README + cookbook.md with pattern recommendations and benchmarking notes
acceptance_criteria: Four repo folders (nextjs, fastapi, go-server, cli) each with runnable example and README
Streaming examples expose both streaming and non-streaming fallbacks and include short note on browser compatibility
Default retry library/config uses exponential backoff with jitter; idempotency key policy demonstrated in server examples
Tests that simulate transient 500 errors and confirm client retries stop after circuit-breaker threshold
Code samples use current Redwood SDK idioms (streaming iterator in Python, ReadableStream in TS, context + channel in Go)
Cookbook document contains concrete decision points: when to enable aggressive batching vs low-latency path
notes: Decision: Python SDK will ship both sync (requests-based) and async (httpx/async-compatible) examples. Rationale: many backend users prefer sync for simple services, but streaming ergonomics require async for efficient resource use.

Trade-off: In Next.js we prefer streaming via Web Streams API (ReadableStream) for modern browsers, but include a lightweight SSE/polling fallback for legacy clients and serverless environments with limited streaming support.
Retry policy chosen: base 100ms, max 5s, multiplier 2.0, jitter 0.25; abort after 6 attempts. This balances transient infra flakiness with not delaying user-visible errors.

Idempotency: examples attach an Idempotency-Key header for non-GET calls; FastAPI example demonstrates server-side storage of key -> response mapping with TTL 1h. Note: production customers should route idempotency writes to durable store (Redis/Postgres).
Batching hint: examples include optional 'x-redwood-batch-hint' header to suggest grouping compatible short requests; documented in cookbook as advisory only (not enforced by runtime).

Observability: each example emits a simple span/event to console for 'stream-start', 'retry', 'retry-failure', 'stream-complete' to help users detect regressions locally. Recommend instrumenting with OpenTelemetry in production.
Security: examples avoid persisting API keys and show pattern for loading from environment/KMS; security_review_required=false for examples but flagged for review if adopted in corporate templates.
